sourceTitle: FOMO: The English We Speak
description: Rob đi xem rock mà không rủ Feifei — ai mới là người có FOMO? Kết thúc bất ngờ, rất vui.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak from BBC Learning English. I'm Rob...
And hello, I'm Feifei.
We're here to teach you a real English phrase...
Rob, what's that you're holding there?
Oh this... just a ticket to see one of my favourite rock bands in concert - The Rolling Thrones.
Oh great - and I see you've got more than one ticket.
Yes, that's right, a few of us from the office are going - it's tonight!
I'm very excited.
Oh right - Rob, it sounds fun - maybe I could get a ticket and join you?
Why? You don't like rock music and you always stay in and wash your hair on a Thursday or so you tell me anyway.
Oh Feifei, I think you've got FOMO.
I've got 'FOMO'?
Is that bad?
Is that why you didn't invite me?
Oh dear, should I go and see a doctor?
No, don't see a doctor.
FOMO is an acronym for 'fear of missing out'.
It's a worried feeling you have that other people are doing fun things when you are not - you're missing out!
Oh, we'd better hear some examples of other people with FOMO...
I know Martha's got FOMO, she's been moaning about not being invited to Wang's karaoke party - but she doesn't even like karaoke!
All my friends are going on holiday together but I can't afford it so I've got FOMO.
There's a message on Facebook that all the tickets to that gig are sold out now I have a feeling of FOMO!
So that's FOMO - fear of missing out which describes a feeling you might have when you feel other people are doing something fun, when you are not.
Well Rob, now I know what it means, I know I haven't got it.
I just wanted to be sociable, and have some fun with you all.
Sorry Feifei, even if you could get a ticket, it's boys only I'm afraid.
Oh look, I've got a message on my social media feed...
is the lead singer of your band called Mick Dagger?
Yes, that's him - the finest rock singer around - why?
It says here, he's fallen down the stairs and broken his leg.
The rock concert is cancelled!
Cancelled? Oh no.
Err, what did you say you were doing tonight?
Washing my hair.
Any chance I could come round...
watch a movie, get a takeaway?
Oh dear Rob.
Have you got FOMO now? Bye. Bye.

title: To cut a long story short…
sourceTitle: To cut a long story short: The English We Speak
description: Rob về nhà lúc 2 giờ sáng và chỉ kể "to cut a long story short…" — nhưng Feifei đã biết hết sự thật!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak from BBC Learning English. I'm Rob...
And hello, I'm Feifei.
We're here to teach you a real English phrase.
Rob, if you don't mind me saying, you look a bit... rough.
Rough? Well you would be, if you'd had the night I've just had.
Oh yes? What happened?
Well, I went out for dinner with Neil, then we went to the pub and then I lost my wallet and...
to cut a long story short...
I got home at two o'clock this morning.
Oh dear. But why 'cut the long story short'?
I want to hear the whole story.
No, you don't - it would take too long and we haven't got time - and anyway,
it's not that interesting - that's why I'm just telling you the most important parts of the story.
Right, so 'to cut a long story short' means to tell only the main or important parts of a story - not all the details.
Hmm, that's a shame Rob because I'm sure you had lots more to tell me.
Really? Well we've got to keep this programme short so shall we move on and hear some examples of this phrase in action...
So I spoke to the boss and to cut a long story short, I'm getting a promotion!
There was a technical problem with our plane which they couldn't fix so to cut a long story short,
we had to wait for another flight and we arrived a day late.
I met Geeta last year and to cut a long story short, we getting married tomorrow!
So 'to cut - or make - a long story short' means to tell only the important parts about something that has happened and leaving out all the details.
So Rob, you're telling me you went out with Neil, lost your wallet and got home very very late?
Yes, that's about it.
Not very exciting, is it?
But the details are boring - that's why my long story is short.
Why do keep asking?
Well actually Rob, it sounds like you're telling a tall story a tall story - a story or fact that is difficult to believe.
Oh really, why do you say that?
Well I spoke to Neil this morning and he said you didn't go for dinner last night.
You went straight to the pub, then another and another pub.
And you left your wallet there so you had no money to get home and had to walk.
Ah well... that's the long story.
Did you really want all the details?
Oh yes. Never cut a long story short if it's a good one!
If you say so Feifei. Bye. Bye.

title: Part 1: "Do you drive a lot?" — from simple to better
sourceTitle: Do you drive a lot?
description: Video ngắn: Keith trả lời cùng một câu hỏi Part 1 ba lần, mỗi lần một hay hơn — từ "I drive to work every day" đến "commute", "a day trip", "a full tank of petrol".

segments.text: Do you drive a lot?
No. I drive to work every every every day.
And maybe at at the weekend.
But that's it. No. I don't drive too much.
Uh I drive to work every day.
And then at the weekend sometimes we drive to a park near our home.
Not really. I commute to work every day.
But that's not too far.
And then sometimes um I drive with my family for a day trip at the weekend.
Usually a full tank of petrol can last me at least a month.

title: Part 1: Desserts — Band 1 to Band 9 answers
sourceTitle: IELTS Band 1-9 | What desserts do people eat in your country?
description: Video ngắn vui: một câu hỏi Part 1, chín câu trả lời từ Band 1 ("Desserts?") đến Band 9 ("quintessentially British", "piping hot"). Nghe từng bậc nâng cấp từ vựng thế nào.

segments.text: What desserts do people eat in your country?
Desserts? Like sticky toffee pudding.
People eat sticky toffee pudding.
It is sweet. I like it.
In my country, people eat sticky toffee pudding.
It is a cake with sauce.
It is very sweet and people like eating it.
A popular dessert in my country is sticky toffee pudding.
It is a type of warm cake with a sweet sauce.
People often eat it in restaurants, especially in winter.
I would say sticky toffee pudding is one of the most popular traditional desserts in the UK.
It is basically a soft sponge cake served with a rich toffee sauce, usually alongside custard or vanilla ice cream.
As it is quite warm and filling, people tend to eat it more often in winter.
One dessert that is particularly popular in the UK is sticky toffee pudding.
It consists of a moist sponge cake covered in a rich toffee sauce
and this is normally served warm with custard or a scoop of vanilla ice cream.
It is quite a heavy dessert, so I think it is more appealing during the colder months.
If I had to pick one quintessentially British dessert, it would probably be sticky toffee pudding.
It is made from a moist sponge cake and covered in a rich buttery toffee sauce.
It tends to be served piping hot with custard or vanilla ice cream.
Although it is undeniably heavy, that's part of its appeal, particularly on a cold winter's evening.

title: Part 1: Weekends — Band 1 to Band 9 answers
sourceTitle: Band 1-9 in IELTS. What do you like doing at the weekend?
description: Video ngắn vui: "What do you like doing on weekends?" — từ "Weekends. I like weekends." đến "sleep in", "at a leisurely pace", "to my heart's content".

segments.text: What do you like doing on weekends?
Weekends. I like weekends.
Weekends, I like to sleep.
Weekends, I like to read.
I like sleeping and reading at the weekend.
At the weekend, I like to sleep and then spend the morning reading a book.
Well, my favorite thing to do is to sleep in at the weekend.
After that, I usually like to have a leisurely morning reading my book.
Well, my favorite way to spend the weekend is to sleep in and then take the day at a leisurely pace.
Usually just reading and enjoying a good coffee.
Well, I totally love having a completely unplanned,
spontaneous weekend where I sleep in and then do nothing but read and drink coffee to my heart's content.
Honestly, the fewer things I have to do, the better.

title: Part 1: Friends or family? & your morning routine
sourceTitle: 15 Most Common IELTS Speaking Questions (with Answers)
description: Hai câu Part 1 rất hay gặp, Keith trả lời mẫu rồi giải thích: to tell you the truth, strive, neglect, a brisk walk, without fail, on my own vs by myself.

segments.text: Question number eight. "Do you prefer to spend time with friends or family?"
This is one of those either or questions and you are like, "both."
Here we go. That's hard to say.
I enjoy spending time with both to tell you the truth.
I'd probably say, overall, I strive to spend more time with my family,
and I guess that means, yeah, sometimes I do neglect my friends.
Okay, so here, yeah, to tell you the truth is just...
It's a filler and it means to be honest or speaking frankly.
Here, of course, the answer's both.
To strive means to try hard to do something.
I strive to spend time with family.
Neglect here means to ignore or not pay attention to.
So I do neglect my friends.
I neglect my friends. Okay, great.
Question number nine. "What's your morning routine?"
Well, I aim to get up at seven o'clock then I go for a brisk walk every morning without fail.
Then I get back, I tend to have breakfast on my own because everyone's asleep and after that I start work.
Okay, so here, to go for a brisk walk, to go for a walk.
Brisk just means fast or quick.
A brisk walk without fail.
It means every day like religiously.
Come rain, come shine, without fail.
And then when we're talking about routines, we often say I typically do this, I tend to do this, I usually do this.
So I tend to have breakfast on my own.
That means without anybody else.
There are two ways to say this, on my own or by myself.

title: Part 1: Work — when you KNOW you are Band 9
sourceTitle: When you KNOW you are IELTS Band 9
description: Video ngắn vui: thí sinh trả lời ngắn, rồi tự "nâng cấp" thành câu Band 9 — my student days are behind me, a fulfilling job, the night shift, all messed up.

segments.text: Do you work or are you a student?
I work. I work as a nurse.
I'm afraid my student days are behind me.
I've been working as a nurse for the last 6 years.
What do you like most about your work?
I like helping people. I like helping people in need.
I'd say I like being able to help people that are in need.
It's a very fulfilling job when you see the impact that you make to people's lives.
Is there anything you would like to change about your work?
The work schedule. I work too many hours and I'm often tired.
I wish I didn't have to work such long hours.
I often start work first thing in the morning and don't finish until last thing at night.
Twice a week I also have to work the night shift, which means that my sleep routine is all messed up.
Do you miss being a student?
No, not really, no. I prefer working.
Not really. There are lots of things that I miss about being a student, such as attending lectures and working on assignments.
But overall, I'm much happier working as I feel that I'm making a greater impact on the world.

title: Part 1: A real Band 9 candidate — hometown & happiness
sourceTitle: Real IELTS Band 9 Candidate answers Part 1 Questions
description: Thí sinh Band 9 thật (Romania) trả lời Part 1 tự nhiên: I'm inclining towards yes, absolutely adore, making up scenarios, feel at ease, serene.

segments.text: Do you live in a large city or a small town?
I live in the second largest city in Romania called Cluj.
Have you lived there for your entire life?
Actually, yes. I know it's quite surprising because there are a lot of people coming from different cities here,
but I've been living here since I was born.
And would you like to continue living here in the future?
Oh, this is an interesting question.
I think yes. I really like the atmosphere.
Everybody's so nice and friendly and we have a lot of nature, which I absolutely adore.
But there's also this idea of wanting to go out outside of Romania and trying to experience different cultures.
So, I'm not quite sure yet, but I'm inclining towards yes more.
Let's move on. Let's talk about happiness.
What made you happy when you were younger?
Oh, I think toys. I was the type of kid that absolutely loved anything that had to do with imagination.
So, I really like making up scenarios and toys were the one friend that could help me do this.
So, I think toys, dolls mostly.
Is there anything that has made you feel particularly happy lately?
Lately, I think I would say books.
I really enjoy reading any sort of reading.
And books just have this tendency of making me feel at ease
and this way kind of I get to feel very serene and happy while I'm reading.

title: Part 1: Cafés — a 17-year-old Band 9 candidate
sourceTitle: Incredible Band 9 Speaking Test (she's only 17!)
description: Trích bài thi thử Band 9 của Sia (17 tuổi): the hum of background conversations, word-of-mouth recommendations, a loyal clientele, media presence.

segments.text: Let's move on. Let's talk about cafes.
Do you have a favorite cafe?
Sure. It is a place right near my house.
It's a warm, cozy place.
What makes it special is the friendly atmosphere there.
Also I love the attention and love with which the staff make each cup of coffee.
It makes the experience even more enjoyable.
Do you often go to cafes by yourself?
Yes, I find cafes to be a perfect place to work and or unwind with a book because the hum of background conversations coupled with some soft music,
they give you the feeling of concentration without the feeling of isolation.
What do you think helps to make a cafe popular?
Well, there are several factors that make a certain cafe popular among people.
The first that immediately springs to my mind is a word of mouth recommendations.
I mean, if a cafe has good food there, good service and etc.
People would be more likely to visit it again probably with their friends.
So, it would help to grow it a loyal clientele.
Also we have to consider that since we live in a digital era era it is important to pay attention to media presence.
So if cafes make their Instagram, Tik Tok or even maybe YouTube pages more attractive to visitors,
it can play a significant role in their popularity.
Why do some people prefer cafes that are part of larger chains rather than small local independent cafes?
Wow, that's a really interesting question.
Probably because international cafe chains, they are they seem more reliable to people because they already know what to expect
and usually they offer certain conveniences like huge parking spaces or reliable Wi-Fi to their customers.

title: Part 2: What happens if you LIE in IELTS?
sourceTitle: What happens if you LIE in IELTS?!
description: Video ngắn vui: thí sinh định "bịa" chuyến đi Nhật với samurai thật… Có được nói dối trong IELTS không? Lời khuyên: kể chuyện thật rồi thêm chi tiết.

segments.text: Now, in part two, I'd like you to describe a special holiday you have had.
A special holiday? I haven't been on any special holidays.
What am I going to say?
I guess I could just invent a story.
I could talk about a time I went to Japan.
I've always wanted to go to Japan.
I'll talk about how I ate so much sushi that I got sick, and how I met a real-life samurai, and… wait.
What else am I going to say?
And what happens if they ask me more questions about Japan?
Will I get a lower score if I lie?
It's okay to lie in the IELTS test, but to be honest, making up the story on the spot is difficult.
I would recommend that you give a true answer,
and then you can always exaggerate or make up small details as you tell your story.
Actually, I couldn't really think of a particularly special holiday I went on,
but I'd like to tell you about a time I went down south to see my best friend.

title: Part 2: Describe a tool you use at home — model answer
sourceTitle: 3 Steps to a Perfect IELTS Speaking Part 2 Answer
description: Cách kết bài Part 2 thật ngắn, rồi nghe trọn bài mẫu của Keith về chiếc kéo: ergonomic handle, come in really handy, I'd go as far as to say…, kept out of reach.

segments.text: So this is not an essential step, okay?
This is not IELTS writing where you must have the conclusion, but if you can control your time, and you know you are coming to the end of your time,
just one simple sentence to wrap it up, to sum it up, can help communication and just, it feels good, but it's not essential.
And actually it really could be something as simple as this.
"Yeah, so that's it. That's the tool that I regularly use in my home."
That's it. Okay, great. Let's move on and have a look at a complete model answer using these tips.
So the tool I'd like to tell you about is a pair of scissors.
It's a very special pair of scissors that I bought a few weeks ago in a local hardware shop.
They're quite big, larger than the normal size,
with an extra larger ergonomic handle made out of plastic, which makes them really comfortable for using.
Yeah, they weren't cheap either, actually.
Talking about what they do.
Well, clearly scissors are used for cutting material like paper, plastic, even wires.
As for me, I use them for cutting card and paper.
The reason is that I'm a teacher, right?
So I spend a lot of time cutting up flashcards and sticking things together.
So scissors, yeah, they come in really handy actually.
In fact, I'd go as far as to say they are an essential for me.
When it comes to the reason they are useful, well, as I just mentioned, I mean,
I use them for work, but they are very useful because they save me time.
And also the fact that they are comfortable means that I can use them for a long period of time without any aches in my hand.
Also, anybody in the house can use them, although we do have to be careful with our baby daughter,
and make sure that, you know, that they are kept out of reach from her so she doesn't cut herself.
Yeah, yeah, so that's it.
That's the tool I regularly use in my home.

title: Part 2: A place with beautiful views — Band 9 answer
sourceTitle: Incredible Band 9 Speaking Test (she's only 17!)
description: Bài Part 2 Band 9 về dãy Alps (Thụy Sĩ): sprung to my mind, densely populated, virgin forests, lost for words, picturesque scenery.

segments.text: Although I've been to many different places with beautiful scenery,
there is a place that has a special place in my heart and it is the Swiss Alps.
I think the Swiss Alps are famous worldwide for how beautiful the mountains are, especially in the winter.
And I had the opportunity to visit the Swiss Alps last December with my family as we were staying there for a family holiday.
It was a very interesting destination and a very interesting choice that I've made because I got to choose where our family was heading.
And the country that immediately sprung to my mind was Switzerland because I know that Switzerland is known for its gorgeous nature.
And since we visited Switzerland in December, we decided to go to the Alps
and stay in a very small village that is not densely populated.
And that gave us a chance to enjoy the beauty of the mountains fully
because we were able to see huskies running all over the place.
And we were able to go snowboarding and hiking which was very enjoyable
because of the fresh air and the freshness that the Swiss Alps offer.
Since we've been there in December, we got to the airport right after fresh snowfall and that made the experience even more surreal.
We also got to visit a few virgin forests.
The experience is indescribable because the nature there is was unexpectedly beautiful.
I've never thought that I would be lost for words when I saw this scenery.
It was a totally picturesque scenery.

title: Part 3: Don't do this! — talk about people, not you
sourceTitle: IELTS Part 3: Don't do this!
description: Video ngắn vui: thí sinh chỉ nói "I don't like computer games" — sai cách! Part 3 hỏi về người khác; nghe câu trả lời đúng: unwind, quite sociable.

segments.text: Why do some people like to play computer games in their spare time?
I don't like playing computer games.
I've always seen them as a waste of time.
Some people like computer games.
Why do you think this is?
I… computer games. Some people do.
I don't. Okay, let's move on.
In part three of the IELTS test, you're mainly asked about other people.
Examiners will often use phrases like some people, young people, old people, teenagers, managers, people in your country.
Try not to talk about yourself too much.
If you talk about yourself, the examiner may interrupt you or remind you to talk about other people,
and you may even get a lower score.
Watch this. Well, I'd say there are a few reasons why people like playing computer games.
First of all, it can be a great way to unwind after a stressful day of work or school.
Also, playing computer games can actually be quite sociable.
You can play with friends online and have something in common with other people.

title: Part 3: Phrases for the generation gap
sourceTitle: The Generation Gap
description: Video ngắn: cụm từ nói về người già – người trẻ cho Part 3: older people (không nói old people), struggle to relate, see eye to eye, set in your ways, bridge the gap.

segments.text: Useful phrases to talk about older people and younger people.
Just note, we don't usually say old people.
That can be a bit impolite.
We say older people. And this, of course, is the generation gap.
The older generation and the younger generation, there's a gap, right?
Useful phrases. They struggle to relate to each other.
That means they often find it difficult to understand each other.
They have different priorities. They see different things as important.
They grew up in different eras.
Different era just means a different time in history.
Sometimes they fail to see eye to eye.
Meaning they struggle to agree with each other.
To be set in your ways meaning you don't like changing.
You have these old habits.
Some older people are set in their ways.
Mind you, so are some younger people.
And finally, to bridge the generation gap.
Old people, young people, a bridge, help them connect with each other.

title: Part 3: Opinion questions — the REE method
sourceTitle: How to Answer ANY IELTS Speaking Part 3 Question
description: Cựu giám khảo hướng dẫn trả lời câu hỏi ý kiến bằng REE: Respond – Elaborate – Example, kèm bài mẫu "Should children have homework every day?".

segments.text: Do you think children should have homework every day?
Should governments spend more money on public transport?
Do you think people rely too much on technology nowadays?
Opinion questions often begin with phrases like "do you think", "do you agree", "should" or "is it a good idea to".
When you get an opinion question, you can use the REE method to build your answer.
REE stands for Respond, Elaborate, Example.
First respond, give the examiner a clear answer to the question.
You can say "definitely", "I think so", "yes", "generally speaking yes", "probably", "probably not", "I don't think so",
"I wouldn't necessarily say that" or you can use my favourite "it depends" or "it depends on".
Next elaborate, explain your answer and give the examiner a reason.
Useful phrases here include "the main reason is that", "one reason for this is", "that's because" or "I think this is mainly because".
Finally give an example, you can say "for example", "for instance" or "a good example would be".
And remember in part 3 your examples should normally be about people or society in general rather than about your own personal experience.
Let's see how this works.
Do you think children should have homework every day?
Probably not. The main reason is that children need time outside school to relax and develop in other ways.
For example, if a child has several hours of homework every evening,
they may have much less time for exercise, hobbies or spending time with their family.
This is a strong answer because the student first responds clearly with "probably not".
Then they elaborate by explaining why children need time outside school.
Finally, they give a general example showing what could happen if children have too much homework.
So, instead of giving a one-sentence opinion, the student has developed one clear idea into a complete answer.
That's the REE method - Respond, Elaborate, Example.

title: Part 3: Effects questions — "the power of two"
sourceTitle: How to Answer ANY IELTS Speaking Part 3 Question
description: Câu hỏi về hậu quả, ảnh hưởng: chỉ cần 2 ý phát triển tốt. Cụm this can lead to, as a result, in the long term — bài mẫu về công nghệ và giao tiếp.

segments.text: The third question type is effects and consequences.
These questions ask you to explain what happens as a result of something.
You might get questions like "how does advertising affect children?", "what effect has technology had on the way people communicate?",
"what are the consequences of people working long hours?"
A really useful technique for these questions is something I call the power of two.
Instead of trying to think of three or four or five different effects, try to just think of two.
Two ideas are usually enough to give you a well-developed answer and they're also very easy to signpost.
You can say, "there are probably two main effects, firstly,
secondly" or "I think it affects people in two main ways, the first is, the second is".
This makes your answer much easier for the examiner to follow.
It also gives you enough time to actually develop each idea rather than just producing a long list.
Your consequence language includes "this can lead to", "this may result in", "as a result",
"one consequence is", "this means that", and "in the long term, this could".
Let's look at an example.
What effect has technology had on the way people communicate?
I think it has affected communication in two main ways.
Firstly, it has made communication much faster and more convenient.
People can contact someone on the other side of the world almost instantly, which makes it much easier to maintain relationships over long distances.
Secondly, it may have made some forms of communication less personal.
For example, people might send a quick message instead of having a proper conversation, and as a result, some interactions can feel less meaningful.
This is a strong answer because the student introduces two clear effects
and signposts them with "firstly" and "secondly" so the examiner can follow the answer easily.
The student also develops both ideas instead of simply listing them.
The first effect is positive and the second is more negative, which gives the answer some balance.
And notice the consequence language "which makes it" and "as a result".
So when you get an effects or consequence question, remember the power of two.
Choose two strong ideas, signpost them clearly, and develop each one.

title: Part 3: Could robots do all of today's jobs?
sourceTitle: Latest Part 3 IELTS Speaking Questions + Answers
description: Không rành chủ đề vẫn trả lời tốt: I'm no expert, but…, as far as I know — cùng từ vựng emotional intelligence, empathy, a long-term therapist.

segments.text: Do you think that all of today's jobs could be done by robots?
No, I don't think so.
I'm no expert, but I'd say there are a lot of jobs that robots still can't do as well as humans.
I can't imagine that a robot would be able to do jobs that require a lot of emotional intelligence or empathy.
For example, a robot wouldn't be able to look after a child at nursery or become someone's long-term therapist.
Maybe AI will change things, but as far as I know, there are still certain jobs that robots can't do as well as humans.
Okay, let's analyze this answer.
Now, this answer is a very good example of showing uncertainty.
We've got phrases that show the examiner that we don't know that much about this topic,
but we're still having a go answering the question.
We've got things like, "I don't think so.
I'm no expert, but I'd say maybe AI will change things, but as far as I know.
So, these phrases are useful discourse markers for showing the examiner that you don't know that much about the topic.
And that's fine. By using these phrases, you're going to be getting a higher score in your IELTS test.
What about some of the vocabulary that we have in this answer?
Well, we've got I'd say.
Now, I'd say is I would say, and it's a good way to introduce your opinion.
It's like I think or I believe.
I'd say, I would say, I'd say.
We've also got good collocations like emotional intelligence.
So, someone with good emotional intelligence is good at interpersonal relationships.
People often distinguish between IQ, which is your thinking and problem solving intelligence, and EQ, which is emotional intelligence,
which is how you are at responding to people and understanding people's needs and feelings.
We've also got this word empathy.
So empathy is the ability to understand others.
If you're an empathetic person, it means that you can understand how people are feeling.
If you're not empathetic, you might be next to someone that's crying their heart out, totally sad, but you don't feel anything for them.
You're totally separate. So, it's better to be empathetic.

title: Part 3: The beauty industry — Band 9 discussion
sourceTitle: Incredible Band 9 Speaking Test (she's only 17!)
description: Part 3 Band 9: quảng cáo mỹ phẩm và trẻ em — overhyped, a genuine purpose, insecurities, cognitive processes, vulnerable to aggressive marketing.

segments.text: Let's consider first of all the beauty industry.
Now, some people say that beauty products are a waste of money.
What do you think? Well, on the one hand, some products really are overhyped
and they do not they're not worth the hype that they're getting from the audience.
But on the other hand, there are some products that serve a genuine purpose.
For example, they can improve your skin, make your skin brighter, and reduce your acne, for example.
So yeah, while some products are overly estimated and they are not worth the attention that they're getting,
there are many other products that are in fact helpful and useful not only in terms of improving your skin improving your skin
and the way that you look like your natural appearances, but also in boosting your self-confidence.
How do you think the beauty industry advertised their products so successfully?
Well, I believe that the way that the marketing sphere is built and the way that they market their products is very interesting
because the beauty industry itself downplays on the humans' most important need and that's the need to be accepted by society.
So they make up their own insecurities.
They bring up the insecurities in women and they make their products sort of the answer towards the insecurity.
And it's really interesting how they do it because once women feel insecure about something,
they search for a project that solves the problem and it turns out that the solution is their product.
Yes, that's very true. So, do you think that possibly beauty companies should not be allowed to advertise to children?
Probably yes because children's minds are not fully formed yet and their cognitive processes are still developing.
Therefore, they might be way more vulnerable than any other group let's say of people towards these aggressive marketing actions.
So I do believe that children especially young girls should not be a target for marketing campaigns.

title: How (not) to start your IELTS test — Gladiator!
sourceTitle: How (not) to start your IELTS test
description: Thí sinh giới thiệu bản thân như phim Gladiator: "Father to a band four son…" 😄 rồi xem cách mở đầu bài thi đơn giản, đúng chuẩn.

segments.text: Can you please tell me your full name?
My name… You already know my name.
You've got it written on that piece of paper.
My name is Maximus Decimus Meridius.
Father to a band four son, husband to a band five wife.
And I will have my vengeance.
In this life or the next.
Oh, and what should I call you?
Just Max? You can call me Gladiator.
At the beginning of the IELTS test, the examiner usually asks you simple questions and you can just give simple answers like this.
Can you please tell me your full name?
Maximus Decimus Meridius. And what should I call you?
Just Max is fine. Where are you from, Max?
Sparta. Can I see your identification, please?
Here you go. Thank you.

title: That'll teach you!
sourceTitle: That'll teach you!: The English We Speak
description: Feifei đi chơi khuya, sáng ngủ quên, đến muộn và luộm thuộm. "That'll teach you!" = đáng đời, lần sau chừa nhé!

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to The English We Speak with me, Neil and errr... where's Feifei?
Sorry I'm late. Hello!
Goodness, it's not like you to be late.
You're always so punctual and...
smartly dressed. But today you look a mess - If you don't mind me saying.
I do mind you saying, Neil.
It's been a very stressful morning.
I didn't have time to shower, iron my clothes or even have breakfast.
Hmm. Did you get up late by any chance?
Yes, you're right.
I forgot to set my alarm last night.
So I overslept!
Has this got anything to do with you going out last night?
I suppose you're going to tell me you had such a great time, you stayed out later than expected?
Yes, how did you guess?
I had one of the best nights out for a long time - but I'm regretting it now!
Ah well, that'll teach you for staying out late - enjoying yourself!
'That'll teach me'?
I'm not going to school - nobody is going to 'teach me' not to stay out late.
It's just a saying, Feifei.
You might say it to someone to suggest that they should learn the bad effects of doing something and not repeat it in the future.
In other words, your stress this morning is a suitable punishment for staying out late last night - you won't do it again.
You sound like my parents!
These examples might explain the phrase better...
You lent some money to Dan and he didn't pay you back - that'll teach you!
My brother got a speeding ticket for driving too fast down the High Street - that'll teach him!
The footballer got a red card for his bad tackle and now he'll miss playing in the final - that'll teach him!
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English and we're hearing about the phrase 'that'll teach you'
which is said to someone to mean they should learn from the bad effects of what they've done.
I guess we could also say 'it serves you right!'?
Yes, it's a very informal but blunt way of saying 'your suffering is your own fault'.
And for you it's true.
But do you know what, Neil - despite my suffering, I had a really good night out.
Oh did you?
And who did you have this 'great night out' with?
Everyone from the office.
We all went to the pub and then onto a nightclub.
That'll teach you for leaving the office early, Neil.
You left too early and you missed out!
Hmm. That's enough teaching for one day. I'm off. Bye!

title: A walk in the park
sourceTitle: A walk in the park: The English We Speak
description: Neil tự tin chạy 5 km "dễ như đi dạo trong công viên"… rồi về đích thở không ra hơi. "A walk in the park" = rất dễ.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei.
And I'm Neil.
Hey thanks for joining me today, Feifei.
No problem, Neil.
I wanted to give you my support for your first run in the park.
Well, this run in the park is only five kilometres.
I know, but you're not particularly fit and you haven't done much training.
Oh don't worry about that - this will be a walk in the park!
Err Neil - I hope you're not thinking of walking around the park - this is a run, a run in the park!
I have no intention of walking - it's just an expression that means it's easy to do, especially compared to other activities.
I'm glad to hear that because it's just about to start - let's hope you really do find it easy!
Don't worry, I will have finished by the time you hear these examples...
I've been studying for so long, this exam should be a walk in the park.
Oh don't worry about me, I've trekked in the Himalayas, this hill will be a walk in the park!
The job at the bank will be a walk in the park - you studied economics at university!
You're listening to The English We Speak from BBC Learning English - and Neil has been using the phrase 'a walk in the park' to explain that a run in the park is easy,
especially when compared to other activities - like running a full marathon, for example.
But where is Neil now?
...here I am.
Oh, that was hard.
So that run wasn't a walk in the park then?
That's a shame.
Why's that?
Well, I thought that if running in the park was too easy, you could train for next year's London Marathon.
It's over 42 kilometres - that would be no walk in the park.
Err, could we just park that idea, please?!
I'm going to do another activity to keep fit and healthy.
Oh yes, what's that?
Walking. In the park!
Good idea. Bye! Bye.

title: Left on read
sourceTitle: Left on read: The English We Speak
description: Roy đọc tin nhắn mà không trả lời vì… đang ăn chuối. Đến khi biết tin nhắn mời đi xem nhạc miễn phí thì đã muộn!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak with me, Feifei… ..and me, Roy.
In this programme, we have an expression which describes when someone has read the message you’ve sent them, but hasn’t replied.
That reminds me, Roy - did you get my message yesterday?
Oh… yes, I did.
I read it and then totally forgot to answer you.
Was it something important?
I can’t believe it!
You completely ignored my message.
I got left on read!
What’s the colour ‘red’ got to do with the fact I forgot to reply?
Red is actually my favourite colour.
Not red the colour, but ‘read’ as in the past of ‘read’.
Ahhh, got you.
Sorry, I didn’t mean to leave you on read.
It’s just I was in the middle of something … and then I got distracted ….and then… OK.
Roy. I understand!
What was so important that you couldn’t reply?
I was eating a really nice banana, and then I just forgot… sorry.
That’s a terrible excuse – it’s a good thing we’re friends or I might think you were ignoring me.
Anyway, let’s listen to these examples…
I can’t believe I was left on read.
I sent him a message and I can see he’s looked at it, but he hasn’t replied!
My partner always leaves me on read.
They get really distracted and then don't message me back.
You shouldn’t assume the worst if you get left on read.
If someone reads your message and doesn’t reply, they might be really busy and planning to respond later.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English and we’re talking about the expression ‘left on read’.
We use this when someone has read a message, but hasn’t replied.
So, were you really eating a banana and that’s why you left me on read?
Yeah, sorry. Well, I was also playing video games which might have been the main reason.
Haha – I knew it!
Well the next time I want to offer you free tickets to the ‘Rob’s Rolling Biscuit’ rock concert,
hopefully you’ll reply and not just leave me on read!
What!?! Free tickets?!
Let me read the message again!
Can I still have the tickets?
Sorry, it’s too late now.
I gave them to Neil.
He didn’t leave me on read.
Bye, Roy. Bye.

title: The best of both worlds
sourceTitle: The best of both worlds: The English We Speak
description: Rob khoe được cả nhịp sống thành phố lẫn bình yên ở quê — cho đến khi tàu về làng bị huỷ. "The best of both worlds" = vẹn cả đôi đường.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak, with you Rob...
...and you, Feifei.
Hey Rob, how are you enjoying your new life in the countryside?
It's great Feifei.
When I get home at night, I get to smell the fresh air and look out on green fields.
Yes, the country life is for me.
But come on Rob, you must miss the bright lights and the excitement of living in the city?
Well, I get that by coming to work right here in the centre of London.
I have a great night out and then slip off to the peace and quiet of the country. Perfect!
Perfect? I don't think so - the countryside is too quiet.
The city is the only place for me.
No way. I've got the best of both worlds - excitement in the city, relaxation in the country.
The best of both worlds - you think you get the advantages of two very different things at the same time.
Yes that's right.
Let's hear some examples of the phrase 'the best of both worlds' in action...
Working part-time means I get the best of both worlds: time with the kids and a steady income.
Our hotel is by the beach and just a short train ride away from the city, so we get the best of both worlds.
We get the best of both worlds with our new car: excellent fuel efficiency and great acceleration and speed.
So the phrase 'the best of both worlds' means you have the benefits of two different things and none of the disadvantages.
But surely Rob there must be some negative things about living in the country?
Such as?
No shops, no pubs or clubs, having a long commute to work every day.
I can cope - anyway, commuting by train is fine - time to relax and shake off the stress of the city.
Maybe not today Rob.
Why? My news feed says there's been a major signal failure - all trains to your village are cancelled!
Cancelled? Grrr. So I can't get home!
Err, any chance I could sleep on your sofa tonight?
Ha, so maybe it's not always possible to have the best of BOTH worlds Rob?
Maybe! Bye. Bye.

title: A wake-up call
sourceTitle: A wake-up call: The English We Speak
description: Rob đi muộn, thở hổn hển vì chạy ra ga. Feifei bảo đây là "a wake-up call" — không phải chuông báo thức đâu, mà là lời cảnh tỉnh!

segments.text: Hello everyone. This is The English We Speak with me, Feifei… and… oh no, Rob is late again!
Sorry I’m late, I missed my train and I had to wait for the next one… Are you OK, Rob?
You’re very breathless.
Well, you would be if you had run to the station and from the station to the office.
Hmmm, it’s not that far, Rob!
I think this is a wake-up call.
A wake-up call?
No, I set my alarm – I got out of bed – it just seems to take longer to walk to the station these days.
I didn’t mean your alarm, Rob.
‘A wake-up call’ is a warning that you need to change your current situation before it gets any worse.
And what is my ‘current situation’?
You’re unfit – you need to do some more exercise!
Let’s hear some examples of ‘a wake-up call’ shall we?
Martha’s bad test results were a wake-up call for her to work harder before her final exams.
The store’s poor sales results are a wake-up call for the business to move with times and sell more fashionable clothes.
The recent extreme weather is a wake-up call for us all to do something about climate change.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English, and in this programme we’re learning about the phrase ‘a wake-up call’,
which means a warning to change your current situation and stop things from getting any worse.
It’s time to change - like Rob’s fitness!
So Rob, how are you going to change your current situation?
Well, that’s easy – I’m going to get a later train.
More time in bed!
I wouldn’t, Rob – otherwise you’ll get another ‘wake-up call’.
Who from? The boss – he hates people being late all the time.
So if you’re not punctual, you might get the sack!
Oh right, I’m off!
Where are you going?
To do some exercise.
Like you said, I need to get fit – quickly!
Bye. Good luck, Rob.

title: Catch-22
sourceTitle: Catch-22: The English We Speak
description: Feifei trượt phỏng vấn vì thiếu kinh nghiệm — nhưng không có việc thì sao có kinh nghiệm? "Catch-22" = tình huống không lối thoát.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak.
It's Feifei here…
…and hello, it's Rob here too.
Oh Feifei, why the glum face?
I didn't get it.
Get it?
I didn't get the job.
Oh yes yes, the job – you went for a new job – one you really really wanted.
One that you said would be perfect for you.
Clearly I am not.
Look at this rejection letter, it says I did not have enough experience.
How dare they!
But if I don't do the job, how do I get the experience?
Oh dear, it sounds like catch-22.
Catch-22? Is that some kind of qualification I need?
Nope, it just describes a situation where you can't win.
Basically, you can't do one thing until you have done another thing which you can't do until you have done the first thing.
So it's an impossible situation.
It is. Let's hear some examples of this phrase in action…
I need my parents' car, but my mum says I need permission from my dad,
then my dad says I need permission from my mum.
I can't get permission from either.
So I'm in a catch-22 situation.
To apply for a short-term student visa to study English in the UK,
you have to be able to speak some English but you want to come to England to learn English!
It's catch-22 for many potential students.
You're listening to The English We Speak and Rob has told me I'm in a catch-22 situation.
That's a situation I cannot win.
Yes Feifei, so you can't get a new job without some experience of doing it
but you can't get the experience without doing the job.
So it's catch-22!
It's a strange phrase Rob.
Yes, it comes from the title of a book, Catch-22,
written by Joseph Heller in 1961 which describes bureaucratic constraints on soldiers in World War II.
But look Feifei, don't be too sad about the job, you've got plenty of experience for doing this job.
That's because I've been here for 40 years!
But we respect you for expertise, especially in one task.
What's that?
Making the tea.
Now could you put the kettle on please?
Oh, I really need a new job.
Bye. Bye.

title: Not gonna lie
sourceTitle: Not Gonna Lie: The English We Speak
description: "Not gonna lie, you look tired" — tiếng lóng để nói thật lòng (hoặc tự khen). Neil và Feifei tranh nhau làm "best presenter".

segments.text: Welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Neil.
And I'm Feifei.
You're a pretty polite person, aren't you, Feifei?
Well, thanks. I don't know.
I do try to be!
That was a very polite answer!
But sometimes we want to say things that are very honest, or that others might not want to hear.
For example, I ask you: "Do I look tired today?"
Well, I could directly say: "Yes, you do look a bit tired."
Or you could start with today's slang expression 'not gonna lie'.
Not gonna lie Feifei, you do look a little tired.
I know, I need to get to bed earlier!
'Gonna' of course, is short for 'going to'.
Using this phrase indicates that you're choosing to be honest rather than polite.
It's not only used for honest criticism, we might also use it before something we're very proud of, or something we boast about.
For example: I love recording these programmes.
Though I'm not gonna lie, I'm the best presenter in this team.
Whoah, that's enough.
I'm sure everyone listening agrees that I'm the best presenter.
Of course you're a fantastic presenter, Feifei.
Just an example!
Talking of examples, let's hear a few more.
Fancy coming round for dinner tomorrow?
Absolutely. If you're making your famous roast?
Oh yes. Not gonna lie, it's the best roast in town!
Slow down! You really are a terrible driver Mark, not gonna lie.
Not gonna lie, I absolutely love my job.
I feel so happy when I walk through the office door every day.
That last example sounds just like me.
Especially as I'm the best presenter.
OK, OK, that joke is getting old now.
You're right. OK, one more thing.
This phrase 'not gonna lie'...
Yes? Not gonna lie, I think some people use it too much!
Yes, it's become a popular phrase on social media.
Usually accompanied by a photo of someone on holiday at the beach with a post saying "Not gonna lie, it's stunning here!"
The kind of post that makes me feel jealous when I'm stuck in the office.
But I thought you loved your job?!
Oh, I do.
And yes, you are a very good presenter, Neil.
That makes me feel much better, not gonna lie. Bye.

title: Barking up the wrong tree
sourceTitle: Barking up the wrong tree: The English We Speak
description: Feifei nghi Rob mách sếp chuyện cô làm đổ cà phê. Rob: "You're barking up the wrong tree!" = nghi nhầm người rồi.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei...
And I'm Rob.
Hello. Errr, Feifei, you're looking a bit angry.
Me, angry! I am angry.
Oh no, what's the problem?
I think you know Rob.
Somebody told the boss that I spilt coffee over his computer yesterday - and now he's angry with me.
Oh no. What kind of mean and horrible person would try and get you into trouble?
You and the boss were the only people left in the office last night. Hmmm?
Whoa - hold on Feifei.
If you are implying it was me who told the boss, then you are barking up the wrong tree.
Please don't make me any angrier by saying that I am like a dog!
No, no Feifei.
Just calm down.
I should be angry because you are making the wrong assumption about who told the boss, OK?
That's what I mean by barking up the wrong tree - you want to blame someone but you got the wrong person.
I didn't even know you had done it.
OK, I'm sorry.
So the phrase 'barking up the wrong tree' means making the wrong assumption when trying to achieve something.
Shall we hear some examples while I make you a coffee to say sorry...?
If you think I have enough spare cash to pay for your holiday, then you're barking up the wrong tree.
You're barking up the wrong tree if you think I was the one who said you were leaving.
It wasn't me!
You're barking up the wrong tree if you think I'm going to lend you my car.
I've seen how you drive!
You're listening to The English We Speak.
We're talking about the phrase 'barking up the wrong tree'.
It means to make a wrong assumption about someone or something.
The phrase can also mean doing something in a way that will not work - you're basically wasting your time.
Like a detective trying to solve a crime by obviously arresting the wrong man - he's barking up the wrong tree.
Ok Rob understood - and here's your coffee to say sorry for barking up the wrong tree.
Thanks - make sure you don't spill it this time.
The boss would be really angry!
...what did I say?
If I find out you did tell the boss, I'll make sure to bark up the right tree, OK?
Oh Feifei, I hope your bark is worse than your bite. Bye. Bye

title: Up your game
sourceTitle: Up your game: The English We Speak
description: Neil nhờ Feifei viết tin nhắn mời bạn gái đi cà phê: "you need to up your emoji game!" = phải nâng trình lên. Kết thúc bất ngờ!

segments.text: Welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Neil.
And I'm Feifei.
Actually, Feifei, can you help me with something?
Go on.
There's this girl I like.
I want to ask her for coffee.
But I don't want to seem too serious or creepy or anything. Just friendly.
And you're writing her a message? OK.
I just can't find the words.
Easy. Stick a couple of emojis on there.
Much less formal!
You mean, like, a smiley face?
Yeah, but those are so last year.
Maybe a love heart?
Seriously? That's a bit too much.
You need to up your emoji game!
My emoji game...
like an emoji of a video game...
or a football?
No. The phrase 'to raise your game', or 'to up your game', means to improve.
Yes, it's a good phrase.
Feifei, you're not working hard enough, you need to up your game!
That's not true...
but good use of up your game.
The phrase has now developed a bit.
We often add what we're trying to improve before the word 'game'.
Like this:
I never finish novels.
I need to up my reading game.
I badly need to work on my interview game before my big interview next week.
You could do with a bit more exercise, mate.
You should raise your running game!
Great. Hope those examples help.
Any progress with that text message?
Here goes: "Lucy.
Please have a coffee with me tomorrow.
And then some coffee emojis.
Well, it's direct!
But I still think we need to up your emoji game.
Actually, and your texting game.
Oh, and your dating game...
We've got a lot of work to do!
Oh, ok. Well I already sent the message.
Let's hope it works!
And she's replied already.
No way, what did she say?
Neil. I thought you'd never ask!
I'd love to have coffee.
3pm?" And then a couple of big smiley emojis.
Wow, congratulations. Maybe it's me who needs to up my game.
Looks like it! Bye.

title: Don't rub it in!
sourceTitle: Rub it in: The English We Speak
description: Feifei bảo Neil "don't rub it in" (đừng nhắc mãi nữa) — và Neil… không thoa kem chống nắng. Về như con tôm luộc!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak.
I'm Neil and joining me in this programme is Feifei.
Hi. Beautiful day today, isn't it?
Blazing sunshine. It's so warm.
Yes it is, and luckily for you, your shift is finished after this programme, isn't it?
Yep! But you have to stay here till evening on the late shift.
Ahhh I'm off to the park to enjoy the sun.
I'd better buy some sun cream, eh?
Don't rub it in!
OK. See you later.
Two hours later.
My word, Neil!
What's happened to you?
You look like a lobster!
It's very hot and sunny out there.
But what about the sun cream?
You told me 'not to rub it in' Feifei!
OK, I think I need to explain something.
We use the expression 'to rub something in' when a person keeps mentioning something another person wants to forget.
When I said 'don't rub it in' I was fed up of hearing about your wonderful afternoon in the sun while I'm stuck here in the office!
Ah. So I actually should have rubbed in this sun cream.
Let's hear some examples...
Don't rub it in.
I know you beat me at tennis but you don't have to keep mentioning the score.
Carlos got into Oxford but I didn't.
That's bad enough, but he keeps rubbing it in by talking about it all the time.
This is The English We Speak and in this programme we're learning the phrase to 'rub it in'.
If a person 'rubs it in' it means they keep mentioning something another person wants to forget.
I want to forget that I've got such a terrible sunburn.
Well I won't rub it in and talk about that sun cream you should have...
should have rubbed in.
Thanks Feifei. Ouch!
Bye! Bye!

title: Why are you having a go at me?
sourceTitle: Have a go: The English We Speak
description: Áo chưa là, dính sốt cà chua, chưa cạo râu… Feifei "has a go at" Neil (chê trách). "Have a go" còn có nghĩa là "thử làm".

segments.text: Morning Neil. In a rush today, were you?
Just a bit, Feifei.
You know, kids, breakfast, commute.
The usual. Why?
Well - I noticed your shirt isn't ironed.
Very attentive of you.
And your shirt has ...
ketchup on it?
Oops, yes - beans for breakfast.
And you haven't shaved, have you?
Well, no. Erm...
You really do need to make more of an effort.
Feifei, why are you having a go at me?
Relax, Neil. I'm just giving you the opportunity to use the phrase we are teaching, which is: 'have a go'!
Well that's a relief.
'To have a go at someone', as we've just seen, means to criticise someone.
That's right. Here are some examples.
The boss really had a go at Michaela after she offended our clients.
Susie had a go at her husband last night.
He'd forgotten all about her birthday.
Why do you always have a go at me?
Why can't you say something nice?
That's our phrase.
'To have a go at someone' - which means to criticise someone.
There. Can we be nice to each other now?
Well, we can have a go!
Ah, very clever.
'To have a go' has another meaning - 'to try'.
Yes - if you have a go at something, you try it.
Why don't you have a go at making an example sentence, Feifei?
Ok then. I'm going to have a go at cooking a Thai curry from scratch.
Tasty. 'To have a go' meaning 'to try'.
And one last thing, Feifei.
Do I really look scruffy?
Not at all.
Though you could shave once in a while.
I'll have a go.
Just for you Feifei. Feifei Bye.

title: A taste of your own medicine
sourceTitle: A taste of your own medicine: The English We Speak
description: Feifei bị cảm và uống thuốc vị "dâu" kinh khủng. "A taste of your own medicine" = gậy ông đập lưng ông — và ai mới là người hay sai bảo?

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei…
and I'm Neil.
Hey Feifei, it sounds like you might have a cold?
I think I have – sore throat, blocked nose.
I feel terrible.
That's why I'm taking this medicine.
That's probably a good idea.
Medicine is usually good for making you feel better but how does it taste?
Well, it's supposed to taste of strawberries but to be honest it's just horrible!
That's why I never take the stuff – it's disgusting.
Have you heard the phrase 'a taste of your own medicine'?
No. Does it mean doing something horrible or unpleasant?
Sort of. It describes someone receiving the same, treatment or unpleasant experience that they have given to somebody else.
You know, like you're always bossing people around and then someone starts to boss you around?
I don't know what you mean Neil!
Anyway, it's quite a negative phrase.
It is. Let's hear some examples…
Our boss is so rude to us but finally somebody has answered back and now he's got a taste of his own medicine.
When I meet up with my boyfriend, he's always late
so this time I'm going to give him a taste of his own medicine and turn up late as well.
Deepak is always rude to the teacher but he was really offended when she gave him a taste of his own medicine and was rude back to him!
So that's 'a taste of your own medicine' which describes someone receiving the same treatment that they have given to somebody else. Excuse me!
Oh dear. It sounds like you need to take some more medicine.
If you mean literally taking the medicine, then yes.
But if you mean receiving the same treatment I've given to someone else, then no.
I can't believe you think I am always bossing people around.
I was just giving an example of the phrase.
I would never say you were bossy.
Good. Now why don't you go and make me a nice cup of tea?
Oh, OK, sure. See you.
And don't forget to close the door!
Yes. Sorry. I'll do that right now.
OK. See you later.
Ah, I feel better already. Bye.

title: Out of the loop
sourceTitle: Out of the loop: The English We Speak
description: Neil bỏ lỡ cuộc họp về chính sách "làm việc lành mạnh": không được ngồi, không cà phê… "Out of the loop" = không nắm thông tin.

segments.text: Hello, and welcome to The English We Speak.
I'm Feifei and with me is Neil.
Hi there.
Neil, what are you doing sitting down?
Presenting this programme – like we always do – sitting in a chair.
You clearly don't know about our new healthy working policy – no more sitting down – standing up is better for you!
Oh, alright then, I'll stand up if I have to.
Oh, Neil! No drinking coffee in the studio.
Health and safety!
Obviously, you missed our meeting about the new healthy working policy.
You are clearly out of the loop.
What? There's a loop I have to stand in now?
No, Neil. You missed our meeting where we discussed the new healthy working policy, and now you're out of the loop.
It means you don't have, or are not aware of the knowledge a particular group of people do have.
In other words, you've missed out on something.
Oh, I hate missing out on things.
We'd better hear some examples so I can be 'in the loop' about this English phrase.
I've been out of the loop since I went on holiday.
I didn't know Geeta and Bilal had got engaged!
They kept me out of the loop, so it was a shock to discover that they were moving our sales team to Birmingham!
Please keep me in the loop if you have any more discussions about the building work. Thanks!
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English.
And we're hearing about the phrase 'out of the loop', which describes not having,
or not being aware of the knowledge a particular group of people do have.
The opposite is being 'in the loop'.
But Neil, you are out of the loop.
Yes, yes, yes.
You've made that clear.
I missed the meeting and I don't know about this stupid 'healthy working policy'.
Where were you anyway?
Down at the café.
You know, having a big fry-up.
Eggs, bacon, sausages! Delicious!
So unhealthy! That's got to stop.
Come on, Neil!
Where are we going?
We're going for a lunchtime run with the rest of the team.
It's part of our new healthy working policy!
Urghh! I think I'd rather stay out of the loop from now on. Bye!

title: It's crunch time!
sourceTitle: Crunch time: The English We Speak
description: Rob nói "crunch time", Feifei tưởng là "lunch time" và lấy khoai tây chiên ra nhai rôm rốp. Hóa ra dự án quan trọng là… chọn bánh quy!

segments.text: Hello I'm Feifei and this is The English We Speak.
And hello, this is Rob.
And it's an important day in the office today, isn't it Feifei?
Err, is it?
Yes, it is!
Remember that big project we've all been working on?
Errr. A big project?
Yes, well it's crunch time.
Oh great – I'm starving.
I'll get my crisps.
No, I didn't say 'lunch time'.
I know. You said 'crunch time' – time to start crunching these delicious crisps.
I love crisps.
No, no – I didn't mean it's time to crunch crisps.
Crunch time is an important or critical time when a decisive or difficult decision has to be made.
And it's crunch time for our big project.
If you say so, Rob.
Why don't I finish these crisps while we hear some examples of the expression 'crunch time'?
We've reached crunch time in our relationship – I'm going to ask my boyfriend to move in with me.
I wonder what he'll say?
The team are doing well but come crunch time, will they score that vital goal?
It's crunch time for us tomorrow – that's when we find out if our building plans have been approved.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English.
We're finding out about the expression 'crunch time',
which describes an important moment in a situation where a difficult or decisive decision has to be made.
But, Rob, I'm still not clear why it's crunch time for our big office project?
Come on, Feifei, you know – the project we've been working on for months.
Oh, you mean the biscuit project?
Exactly! We have to decide today which biscuits we're going to buy for our meetings.
And if we don't order them today, we won't have anything to eat in tomorrow's meeting.
So, Rob, your crunch time is just about what you'll be crunching tomorrow.
You really need to change your priorities.
I think I've reached 'crunch time' in this programme.
What's that? You've got a big decision to make?
Yes - to finish this programme or finish my crisps?
Shall we just eat the crisps?
OK. Bye.
Bye. Pass them over then!

title: It's the thought that counts
sourceTitle: It's the thought that counts: The English We Speak
description: Neil tặng Feifei quà Giáng sinh sớm: kính Harry Potter! "It's the thought that counts" = quý ở tấm lòng — cách khen lịch sự món quà mình không thích.

segments.text: Hello and welcome to The English We Speak. I'm Feifei.
And I'm Neil.
Oh what's that parcel you've got in your hands there, Neil?
Looks exciting... It's a present.
A present? For who?
For you! For Christmas!
Christmas? It's a bit early, isn't it?
Well, I saw these and I just knew you'd love them so much - so I bought them!
I can't wait till Christmas to see your face.
Go on, open it now!
You're too kind, Neil.
OK... A pair of glasses...
Harry Potter glasses.
Aren't they brilliant?!
Go on, try them on.
I look ridiculous.
And I don't even like Harry Potter.
Oh well, it's the thought that counts.
'It's the thought that counts'.
An excellent expression, Feifei.
If someone gives you a present which you don't like, you can say 'it's the thought that counts'.
It's a polite way of saying you appreciate the effort and the kind thought a person had when they bought you a present...
but you don't like what they bought.
Let's hear some examples of this expression which is particularly useful around Christmas time.
Wow! That Elvis Presley onesie you're wearing is pretty weird.
Thanks. My grandmother gave it to me for Christmas.
It's the thought that counts, I suppose.
I have no idea what to get my auntie for her birthday.
Get her anything.
It's the thought that counts.
Oh no, not more tea towels.
I was expecting something more exciting for our wedding presents.
You know what they say - it's the thought that counts.
This is The English We Speak from BBC Learning English.
Our expression is 'it's the thought that counts.'
It means the kindness someone shows when they buy you a present is more important than the gift itself.
A very useful expression for politely saying that a present someone bought you is really not what you wanted.
OK, Feifei, lean over.
Ouch! What are you doing with that pencil?
There we go.
With that flash of lightning on your forehead now you really look the part Feifei Potter.
Hmm I need a spell to make you vanish, Neil... Bye! Bye!

title: Numbers: 13 or 30? Teen vs -ty
sourceTitle: Listening Practice Numbers 13 or 30
description: Phân biệt 13–30, 14–40… nghe trọng âm: "-teen" nhấn âm cuối và kéo dài, "-ty" nhấn âm đầu. Mẹo: dùng logic — "bà tôi 17 tuổi" chắc là 70!

segments.text: Hello and welcome to today's IELTS listening practice lesson.
And today we're going to listen to the different sounds with certain numbers.
So the numbers are 13 and 30, 14 and 40.
So we'll see how they are pronounced differently and how you can listen to them and write them down correctly.
So let's look at the two groups. We have "teen", which is a longer sound, and then "ty", which is short, and it is a different vowel sound.
And also, the difference in pronouncing these two different sets of numbers is, for the teen numbers, the last syllable is stressed.
But for 30, 40, the first syllable is stressed.
Okay, so there is a difference in the stress as well as a difference in the sound and the length of the sound.
So now let's have a look and say the teen numbers: 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19.
It's really easy: making it long in the second syllable, and that's the stressed syllable.
We know it's the "teen" and not the other form of the number.
Now I will say the other numbers: 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, 90.
So the first part, the first syllable, is longer and stressed.
Okay, now I will say them together so you can hear the difference, and this is what you need to be aware of in the listening exam.
Okay, there's quite a big difference, so you can use this when you speak to show which number you're saying.
Make it clear. They should be different. They don't sound the same. They are quite different.
And of course, use this in the listening exam when you're listening for the number: think, which number did they say, as well as listening for the actual sounds.
Also, think about the logic.
Okay, if someone says, "My grandmother is 17 years old", that's probably not true.
It's not 17, it will be 70.
Okay, so think about the logic as well as the sounds: the stress, which syllable is stressed.
