so they tend to sound almost perfect even when the singers themselves don't perform that well live.
I think only some top vocalists with excellent live singing ability, like Adele, for example,
can make their voice sound just as good as or even better than the recorded version when performing live.
Do young people prefer modern music events?
Well, I wouldn't say all young people do because there are still those who don't really like crowded and noisy places.
You know, I'm actually one of them.
But for the most part, I do think young people tend to prefer modern music events.
You know, I sometimes come across videos of these events on social media, and they're usually packed with young adults,
especially at music festivals or big concerts, which shows how much they enjoy being at such events.
How important is sound quality at concerts?
It's hands-down one of the most important things at concerts.
You know, a good sound system not only enhances the atmosphere by making the music sound clear and powerful,
but also helps artists feel more confident about their performance, and vice versa.
That's probably why in many big music shows, organizers invest a huge amount of money in the sound system.
And artists also check the sound quality carefully before performing on stage.
Should music events be affordable for everyone?
Ideally, it should be because that way, everyone, especially people with lower incomes, can enjoy good music and see artists they admire.
However, in reality, it would be quite difficult since organizing a music event can be extremely costly, especially for large-scale concerts or music festivals.
You know, organizers have to pay for the venue, the sound system, the staff, and most importantly, the artists.
Some famous artists tend to charge very high performance fees, so if the ticket prices are too low,
organizers and sponsors may struggle to make a profit.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 Band 8 Samples: Describe a time when you needed to use your imagination
title: Part 2: A time you needed to use your imagination
description: Dùng trí tưởng tượng để chuẩn bị bài thuyết trình: visualization, a self-help book, far-fetched, received several compliments, over the moon.

segments.text: Describe a time you needed to use your imagination.
I'm going to talk about the time I had to use my imagination to mentally prepare for an important presentation at university
and it was actually quite a memorable experience for me.
This happened around 3 or 4 years ago when I was a second-year student.
At that time, I was taking a public speaking course and giving a presentation was compulsory if I wanted to pass the subject.
Since speaking in front of an audience had never really been my strong point, I put a lot of effort into preparing for it.
You know, I watched plenty of online tutorials on how to design professional-looking slides.
I also practiced speaking in front of the mirror several times to improve my body language and delivery.
More importantly, a few days before the actual presentation, I tried a technique called visualization, which I'd learned from a self-help book.
Basically, I imagined myself confidently going through each part of the presentation and everything going smoothly.
To be honest, I was quite skeptical at first because it sounded a bit far-fetched.
However, it turned out to be surprisingly effective.
On the presentation day, I delivered the speech almost exactly the way I had imagined and I even received several compliments from my lecturers.
You know, my score was among the highest in the class which made me feel absolutely over the moon.
Since then, I've been using this visualization technique whenever I need to prepare for something important, especially situations that make me feel nervous.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 Band 8 Samples: Describe a time when you needed to use your imagination
title: Part 3: Imagination & creativity
description: Trí tưởng tượng & sáng tạo — 9 câu hỏi: think outside the box, precise data, forming hypotheses, reading vs cartoons, building blocks, role-playing games.

segments.text: Is imagination important to children?
Yeah, absolutely. From my point of view, imagination plays a crucial role in children's development.
That's mainly because it helps them think more creatively
which is especially important in today's world where, you know, innovation is valued across many fields.
Without this ability, children may struggle to see the world in their own way and simply follow expectations set by adults.
What subjects are helpful for children's imagination?
Off the top of my head, I'd say creative subjects, especially art and drawing.
One of the main reasons is that these subjects really push children to use their imagination because, you know, they have to decide what goes into a picture,
what colors to use and even small details that bring everything together.
There's no single right answer which gives kids the freedom to think creatively rather than just follow rules.
That's probably why art is a core subject in schools all over the world.
What kinds of jobs require imagination?
Well, first of all, in this digital age, I'd say imagination is needed in almost every job.
But if I had to single out one profession, it would definitely be content creators.
You know, even the job title itself speaks volumes about what's required.
You constantly have to think outside the box and come up with original ideas in order to, you know, stand out from the crowd.
That's what makes the job fascinating but also mentally demanding at the same time.
Do you think imagination is essential for scientists?
I think imagination is important for scientists but in a more controlled way.
I mean on the one hand science is built on precise data and strict methods.
So scientists can't rely purely on creativity.
On the other hand, imagination is crucial when it comes to forming new hypotheses and exploring new possibilities.
Without that balance between creativity and discipline, scientific progress would either become too rigid or too unrealistic.
Which requires more imagination: reading or watching cartoons?
I'd probably lean a bit more towards reading.
You know, when you read, you're mainly dealing with text and very few, how should I put it, visual cues.
So, you have to rely heavily on your imagination to picture the story.
For example, what the characters look like, how they feel, or where events take place.
By contrast, cartoons already provide all the visuals, which means the director has done most of the imaginative work for you.
As a result, there's generally less room for the viewer's imagination.
What's the relationship between creativity and imagination?
The way I see it, creativity and imagination are closely connected.
You know, imagination helps generate ideas while creativity is about bringing those ideas to life.
The more creative activities people engage in, the more they tend to exercise their imagination.
And the two skills often reinforce each other.
That's why people often discuss them together and sometimes even confuse one with the other.
Do you think adults can have lots of imagination?
Yeah, definitely. In my view, imagination doesn't really depend on age, but rather on how often people use it.
Just like any other skill, if you keep practicing and exercising your imagination, it naturally becomes sharper over time.
So, it's entirely possible for an older person to be more imaginative than a younger one, especially if they regularly do creative work.
And the opposite can also be true.
What games require children to use imagination?
I think there are quite a few games that encourage children to use their imagination,
but one that immediately comes to mind is building blocks.
You know, kids need to think creatively and visualize what they want to create,
whether it's a house, a castle, or even different vehicles like cars or airplanes.
There aren't many fixed rules, so they're free to experiment and come up with their own ideas.
Another good example would be role-playing games.
Since kids create characters and imaginary situations on their own, their imagination plays a key role.
How can teachers encourage children to use imagination?
From my experience, one practical thing teachers can do is design activities or games that, you know, require children to actively use their imagination.
These can be simple tasks like drawing a picture based on something that impressed them
or more complex ones such as acting out a story they have read or watched.
The key point is to give students enough freedom to explore ideas rather than forcing them to follow fixed patterns or rigid rules.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 Band 8 Samples: Describe a sports competition you watched
title: Part 2: A sports competition you watched
description: Chung kết bóng đá SEA Games 33 Việt Nam – Thái Lan: a roller coaster of emotions, conceding two early goals, an unbelievable comeback, the never-give-up spirit.

segments.text: Describe a sports competition you watched.
I'm going to talk about the final match of the 33rd SEA Games between Vietnam and Thailand,
which was an incredibly emotional experience for me.
It took place just a few months ago, so many of the details are still very vivid in my mind.
That day, my family and I watched the match together on TV, and it was honestly a real roller coaster of emotions.
In the first half, Thailand was clearly in the lead, scoring two early goals.
At that point, many Vietnamese fans, including myself, thought we were heading for a, you know, humiliating defeat, and it was hard to hide our disappointment.
However, everything changed in the second half.
Vietnam made, you know, an unbelievable comeback by scoring two goals and one more in the extra time and eventually won the match.
As a result, we became champions and the team brought home another gold medal for the country.
I still remember how thrilled I felt when our striker scored the winning goal and it was absolutely exhilarating.
You know, Thailand has always been one of Vietnam's fiercest rivals in sports, so beating them made the victory sweeter.
After the match, people of all ages poured into the streets, waving flags, honking horns, and celebrating late into the night.
It genuinely felt like the whole country came alive.
What I admire most about this match is the never-give-up spirit and determination of the players.
You know, not many people believed they could turn the game around after conceding two early goals.
Overall, it was an unforgettable match and even talking about it now makes me feel extremely proud.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 Band 8 Samples: Describe a sports competition you watched
title: Part 3: Competitions, prizes & sport on TV
description: Thi đấu thể thao: prizes and incentives, sportsmanship, football attracts the largest audience, broadcast on TV, a sedentary lifestyle.

segments.text: Do you think it is necessary to award prizes and incentives to athletes?
Yeah, I'd say so, especially when athletes are preparing for big competitions because prizes and incentives can really push them to train harder and stay focused.
After all, professional athletes often have, you know, relatively short careers.
So, financial rewards help them feel more like secure and appreciated for their efforts.
That said, I don't think money should be the main driving force.
If athletes start competing purely for financial rewards,
it can take away from sportsmanship and the original spirit of sport where, you know, fair play and personal growth should still matter.
What kinds of competitions do people in your country like to watch?
To be honest, sport isn't something I follow very closely these days, so I can't say for sure.
However, from what I've observed, in Vietnam, sports competitions are generally more popular among men and football in particular attracts the largest audience.
Major tournaments, especially those held in Europe, tend to draw a lot of attention because most of the players are at a very high level and the competition is extremely intense,
which makes the games far more thrilling to watch.
Should more matches be broadcast on TV?
Well, I don't know about others, but for me, it could be a great idea.
I mean, not everyone has enough time or money to go to live matches.
So, if more matches are broadcast on TV, it would make watching sports much more accessible to the public.
Also, when people are, you know, exposed to sport more often, chances are they may be encouraged to try it themselves,
which is especially important nowadays when many of us tend to lead a sedentary lifestyle.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 BAND 8 SAMPLES: Describe an argument two of your friends had
title: Part 2: An argument two of your friends had
description: Hai cô bạn cãi nhau khi làm bài thuyết trình nhóm: critical comments, took it personally, a heated argument, act as a mediator, blocked each other on Facebook.

segments.text: Describe an argument two of your friends had.
Well, this topic reminds me of the time when I was doing a group assignment with some friends at university.
If I remember correctly, it happened around 6 months ago when I was still a second-year student.
There were four of us in the group, two girls and two boys, and I was chosen as the group leader.
To keep things fair, I divided the presentation into four parts and let everyone choose the section they felt most confident with.
We were given about a week to prepare our parts.
And the problem came up during our rehearsal.
One of the girls, Nhung, wasn't satisfied with what Hang had prepared and made a few, you know, critical comments about it.
However, the way she expressed herself was a bit too direct.
So Hang took it personally.
From Hang's point of view, she felt she had already tried her best and that her work wasn't as bad as Nhung made it sound.
At first, it was just a small disagreement, but within a few minutes,
it turned into quite a heated argument between the two of them.
As a group leader, I had to step in and act as a mediator.
I tried to calm them down, explained each person's point of view, and suggested some practical ways for her to improve her part.
Then we went through the rehearsal together again, but the mood was never the same.
In the end, the presentation did go well,
but the two of them didn't really sort things out afterward and even blocked each other on Facebook.
From this experience, I learned that communication skills are incredibly important
because if you're not careful with your words, it can easily damage a relationship.

sourceTitle: IELTS SPEAKING PART 2 + 3 BAND 8 SAMPLES: Describe an argument two of your friends had
title: Part 3: Arguments & disagreements
description: Tranh cãi & bất đồng: talk things through, pet peeves, daily friction, in the heat of an argument, jump down each other's throats, a different take on it.

segments.text: Do you think arguments are important?
Well, I think arguments can be important, but only if they're handled properly.
I mean, if people are willing to sit down afterward, talk things through calmly, and figure out the root cause of the issue,
arguments can actually help them understand each other better and even strengthen their relationship.
On the other hand, if both sides just stick to their own opinions or avoid making amends,
it can slowly take a heavy toll on the relationship over time.
What do family members usually argue about?
Well, I can't speak for everyone, but based on my own family and others around me,
I'd say that family arguments usually revolve around differences in daily habits.
For instance, one person might be a bit messy while another is very neat.
And when people are forced to deal with their pet peeves on a daily basis, it can easily lead to conflict.
Is it easier to argue with family members than with friends?
I suppose so because family members usually live together and see each other every day, so they're more exposed to each other's habits.
With friends, people can keep some distance, but in families,
people don't really hold back and tend to say exactly what they think, which makes it harder to avoid daily friction.
Should people change their way of thinking in an argument?
Ideally, yes. It would be great if people could because that's often the quickest way to end an argument.
You know, if one person is willing to accept the other's point of view, the conflict can stop right there.
That said, in reality, it's quite difficult since most people don't like admitting they're wrong,
especially when they are already in the heat of an argument and not thinking as calmly as they normally would.
Who should teach children to respect teachers?
Off the top of my head, I'd say their parents.
They are the ones who, you know, have the greatest influence on children and the people they look up to the most.
So, their words tend to carry more weight than anyone else.
If it's not parents, I honestly can't think of anyone who should take on that role, at least at this moment.
How can we show respect to others in a disagreement?
From my own experience, one way to do that is to let others finish their sentences.
A lot of the time, people just jump down each other's throats instead of listening to the other person's opinion,
and that usually makes things worse because no one likes being interrupted, right?
Another effective approach is to use phrases like, "I understand your point, but I have a different take on it."
That way, the other person is less likely to feel offended and more willing to listen to your viewpoint.

title: Joe & Bella: Football match
sourceTitle: Football match - The Storytellers
description: Joe được chọn vào đội bóng của trường, nhưng một cậu bé to con cứ chơi xấu — và Bella lao ra sân bênh anh! Từ vựng: pitch, referee, yellow card, trip up, bully, score a goal.

segments.text: Joe loved football.
He played it with his friends at school, in the park with his dad on weekends,
and sometimes he even played it with his little sister, Bella, in their back garden.
She usually missed the ball when she tried to kick it.
But it was better than nothing.
"I wish I could be on the school team," Joe told his friend, Finn.
But maybe because he was small for his age, he never got chosen.
Then one day at break time, when Joe was playing football with his friends, Mr Burton, the football coach, came over.
"How would you like to play for the school team this weekend?" asked Mr Burton.
Joe felt like he was going to burst.
"I'd love it!" he said.
Joe felt so excited that he couldn't wait to tell Mum and Dad.
But there was a problem.
"I'm so pleased for you," said Mum. "But – oh dear –"
"I'm not sure you can play this weekend."
"You see, Dad and I are away, and you and Bella are going to stay with Gran."
Gran lived close by. She often looked after Joe and Bella when Mum and Dad were busy.
"But I've got to," Joe said. "It's my big chance!"
Gran had made plans to take them for a long walk with her dog, Selby, on Saturday morning.
But when she heard, she said she would take Joe to the football match instead.
"Of course, I'll have to bring Bella and Selby too."
Joe wasn't sure about this.
Bella could be such a nuisance.
You never could be sure what she might do!
On Saturday morning Joe found it hard to eat breakfast, he was so nervous.
He gave some of his toast to Selby when Gran wasn't looking.
The football pitch was in the park.
There were lots of kids getting ready, and lots of parents standing at the side to watch.
Some of them had dogs.
The dogs barked at Selby and Selby barked back.
Gran and Bella waved at Joe as he ran onto the field. "Good luck!" they shouted.
Joe was pleased to see that Gran was keeping tight hold of Selby and Bella.
Selby was pulling hard on her lead, and Bella was jumping up and down.
Poor Gran looked close to being pulled in two!
The whistle blew and the match began.
Joe ran up the field with the ball.
He was about to pass it when a big boy from the other team crashed into him.
He was almost twice as big as Joe.
All the breath was knocked out of Joe, and the ball went off the pitch.
Joe hoped the referee would show the boy a yellow card.
But the referee didn't seem to have noticed.
Maybe there had been too many players in the way.
After that, whenever the referee wasn't looking in their direction, the big boy would give Joe a shove.
It made it really difficult for Joe to play well.
The next time the ball came towards them, the big boy stuck out his foot and tripped Joe up.
"Hey!" yelled Finn, as Joe lay on the ground. "Did you see that?"
But the referee said that it had been an accident.
Selby and Bella had seen.
Selby tugged on her lead and barked at the referee.
"Please control that dog," the referee told Gran.
"Or I will ask you to leave!"
Gran was trying so hard to hold Selby that she let go of Bella's hand.
Bella ran onto the pitch and up to the boy who had tripped Joe.
"Don't you dare trip up my brother!" she told him.
"I saw you push him too!"
Joe was really embarrassed. But, to his surprise, most of the parents and players were on Bella's side.
Some of them began to cheer.
"She's quite right," they said.
"That big boy's a bully! It's disgraceful!"
Gran grabbed hold of Bella.
For the rest of the match the bigger boy didn't dare touch Joe. And after fifteen minutes – Joe scored a goal!
"Can I always come and watch you play football?" asked Bella at the end of the game.
And Joe said she could.

title: Joe & Bella: Sick day
sourceTitle: Sick day - The Storytellers
description: Bella kêu ốm để được nghỉ học — hóa ra đã ăn vụng hết hộp kẹo! Còn Joe đau khuỷu tay mà chẳng ai để ý. Từ vựng: sore, tummy, feverish, bruise, X-ray, sling.

segments.text: One morning Joe woke up with a sore elbow.
He prodded it carefully with one finger. Ow! That really hurt!
Joe climbed out of bed and put on his dressing gown, very, very carefully, so as not to joggle his bad elbow.
Then he went downstairs. Mum was in the kitchen, searching for cereal in the cupboard.
"We're out of cornflakes again," she said, not looking round.
"Mum," Joe began, "I think there's something wrong with my -"
But at that moment, Bella came into the kitchen.
She was clutching her tummy.
"Mum," she cried, "I'm very, very ill! Very ill indeed!"
"My tummy hurts really, really bad!"
"I am far too sick to go to school!"
Mum was worried. She felt Bella's forehead.
"You do feel hot. But you were fine yesterday."
"I'm not fine now," said Bella.
"Please, Mum. Can I go back to bed?"
Bella didn't even want breakfast.
Joe tried to tell Mum about his elbow.
But Mum was too worried about Bella.
"Please just get dressed, Joe, or you will be late for school!"
Mum stayed home to look after Bella.
Dad gave Joe a lift to school, and Joe tried to explain about his elbow.
"I was playing football yesterday and I banged it and it still hurts," he said.
"Probably just a bruise," said Dad.
"I hope Bella is better soon."
"She looked a bit feverish to me."
It's always about Bella, thought Joe crossly.
At school, Joe had to be very careful of his elbow.
He had to keep it really still.
Luckily he could still write with his other hand.
At home, Mum was looking after Bella.
She put her back to bed and tucked the covers round her.
She brought her a glass of water to sip slowly.
She stroked her head and read her a story.
"How do you feel now?" she asked.
"Would you like to try a little breakfast?"
"I can't eat a thing," said Bella.
Mum was worried. It wasn't like Bella not to eat anything.
She leaned over to pick Bella's teddy bear off the floor.
As she did so, she caught sight of something under the bed.
A huge pile of sweet wrappers! And an empty box!
"Bella!" Mum cried. "Are those the sweets that Aunt Jackie sent you?"
"And that you were supposed to save for your birthday?"
Bella turned very red. "I woke up early and felt hungry," she said in a small voice.
"But Bella," said Mum, "no wonder you've a bad tummy! You've eaten every one!"
An hour later, Mum and Bella were walking into school.
Bella's tummy was better, and Mum wanted to get back to work.
Mrs Smailes, the headteacher, came running to meet them.
"Oh good, you're here," she said.
"I think you need to go straight to hospital!"
"Hospital!" said Mum. "She's only eaten too many sweets!"
"I'm not talking about Bella!" said Mrs Smailes. "I'm talking about Joe!"
"Didn't you notice that he'd broken his elbow?" "What!" said Mum.
At the hospital, Mum and Joe had to sit in the waiting room, until Joe could have his X-ray.
"Why didn't you tell me?" Mum said.
"I did try," said Joe. "But you wouldn't listen."
"Then my teacher noticed I couldn't move my arm."
At the hospital they were very kind to Joe.
They took an X-ray of his arm, and the doctor showed him the picture of the crack in his bone.
A nurse wrapped up Joe's elbow in a bandage.
Then they put his arm in a sling.
Joe was sad that he wouldn't be able to play football for a few weeks,
so Mum bought him a box of sweets from the hospital shop to cheer him up.
"I hope Bella doesn't steal any," said Joe, opening the box.
"I don't think she will," said Mum, smiling.
"I think she's had enough sweets to last her a long time!"

title: Joe & Bella: Camping
sourceTitle: Camping - The Storytellers
description: Chuyến cắm trại đầu tiên của Bella: dựng lều, nướng marshmallow và tiếng sột soạt bí ẩn ngoài lều lúc nửa đêm. Từ vựng: tent, sleeping bag, pitch a tent, rustling, hike.

segments.text: The Hobson family were going camping.
It was Bella's first camping trip, and though she was excited, she was nervous too.
"What if the tent falls over and squashes us?" she asked Joe.
"It's too light to squash us," said Joe.
"Well, what if the wind blows it away?"
"The wind isn't strong enough."
"Well, what if a wolf comes into the tent and eats us?"
This made Joe laugh. Bella had read too many fairy stories with big, bad wolves in them.
"There aren't any wolves in Yorkshire," he said.
"There aren't any wolves in the whole of Britain."
"Except in zoos, of course."
"Well, what if one escaped from a zoo?" asked Bella.
Joe said that zoos were far too careful to let their animals escape.
And Bella soon forgot about wolves as they started planning for the camping trip.
"Let's get ready, kids!" said Dad, on Saturday morning.
"As soon as we're packed up, then we're off!"
They all helped load up the car.
First, they put in the tent – it was a big one for the whole family.
Then the sleeping bags and blankets.
It's cold at night, when you're sleeping in a tent.
Then they packed the cooking equipment, and lots of food to cook.
When everything was packed, the car was full to bursting.
The Hobson family just managed to squeeze in.
Soon they were leaving the city behind them.
"Look at the hills!" said Dad.
"Look at the heather on the moors!"
They drove up a winding road with no houses until they reached the turning for the campsite.
It belonged to a farm and was in a big field.
There were views out over the moors, and lots of space for people to pitch their tent.
"Right," said Dad. "First things first!"
"Let's get the tent up."
"Here's a good spot, next to this hedge."
Once the tent was up, it was time to eat.
Then Joe and Bella went to explore.
There were trees to climb and a stream for paddling.
Bella started collecting tadpoles in a jar with another girl, and Joe played on a rope swing with some of the older kids.
The day flew by. "Tomorrow," said Dad, "we'll go for a long hike over the moors."
"I can't wait," said Joe.
It was getting dark. The family ate sausages and beans, then roasted marshmallows on sticks over a camp fire.
They drank hot chocolate too.
In the darkness, strange rustling noises came from the hedge next to their tent.
"What's that noise?" asked Bella.
She looked nervous, and moved closer to Mum.
"Don't worry, it's not a wolf," said Joe teasingly. "How do you know?"
"I expect it's just a rabbit, Bella," said Dad.
"Or maybe it's just the wind, rustling the leaves."
Bella didn't say anything more.
Of course she was only little, thought Joe.
You couldn't really blame her for having silly worries about wolves!
"Time for bed," said Mum.
They were all tired after a day outdoors.
They put out the fire, closed the tent flap and crawled into their sleeping bags.
Soon Bella, Mum and Dad were asleep.
Joe was too excited to sleep.
So he lay awake thinking about the day, and wondering what would happen tomorrow.
Suddenly, he heard something from outside the tent.
A rustling noise. "Probably just a rabbit," he thought.
Then he heard more rustling.
It sounded like something walking around outside – something bigger than a rabbit.
What if, thought Joe, Bella was right?
What if a wolf did escape from a zoo?
This campsite was just the kind of place it might like.
Joe lay there, shivering, as the rustling continued.
At last, he could bear it no longer.
He got up and stuck his head out of the tent.
A cow gazed at him over the hedge.
She had soft, brown eyes, and was chewing peacefully on some leaves. "Moo!" she said.
Joe chuckled to himself as he crawled back into his sleeping bag.
"To think I was afraid of a cow!"

title: Joe & Bella: School trip
sourceTitle: School trip - The Storytellers
description: Lớp Joe đi công viên động vật hoang dã nhưng xe hỏng giữa đường cao tốc và khu sư tử lại đóng cửa! Từ vựng: wildlife park, coach, break down, motorway, enclosure.

segments.text: One day Joe's teacher had some news.
"We're going on a school trip," she told the class.
"As we've been learning about different animals, we are going to visit a wildlife park."
Everyone was excited. "Bears!" yelled Finn at playtime. "Rhinos!" "Leopards!" shouted Joe. "Lions!"
That evening, Joe showed his parents the letter about the school trip.
"Wonderful," said Mum. "We must make sure you have everything you need."
"Will there really be lions?" asked Bella, her eyes big with excitement.
"Yes, and leopards too." "Ooh," said Bella, and her eyes grew even bigger.
On the morning of the trip, Joe had everything ready.
He had a backpack with his sandwiches and water bottle.
He had a warm scarf in case it was cold, and sunscreen in case it was hot.
He had a camera to take pictures of the animals.
"Quick," he said at breakfast. "I can't be late."
"Or they might leave without me."
"Don't worry," said Bella. "I'm ready."
"Look, I'm taking some extra snacks in case the animals are hungry."
Everyone looked at Bella. She had a packed lunch, a water bottle, a scarf and sunscreen.
She thought she was going to the wildlife park too!
"But Bella," said Dad, "Joe is going, not you."
"It's a school trip!" shouted Bella.
"I'm part of the school!"
"But the trip is only for the big ones," said Mum.
"I want to see the animals!" howled Bella.
Joe said nothing. Why did his sister always make a fuss, he wondered.
Why did she always try to butt in?
His parents were trying to calm Bella.
"We'll take you to the wildlife park at the weekend."
"Want Joe to come!" Bella wailed.
Joe lost his temper. "It's time you learned you can't have everything your way," he told his sister.
"I'm going on this trip, not you."
"If you go at the weekend – fine – but I'm not coming with you!"
Nothing they said would make him change his mind.
When they got to the school, the coach was waiting.
Joe sat next to Finn.
"I can't wait to see the rhinos," said Finn.
"I like lions best," said Joe. The coach set off.
It had only gone a little way down the motorway when it began to make a strange noise.
It was banging and rattling.
There was smoke coming from the back.
The coach driver pulled to the side of the motorway.
With a thud, the coach stopped!
"We've broken down," said Finn.
The driver phoned the breakdown service.
At first it was exciting, but after a while everyone began to get bored.
"This is no fun," grumbled Finn.
Finally, the breakdown truck arrived.
But it couldn't fix the coach. They waited and waited.
At last, a new coach came.
Everyone had to climb off the first coach and onto the second one.
They were all bored and hungry by now.
When they got to the wildlife park, it was very busy.
There were lots of school groups already there.
They had to wait in line at the gate.
When they finally got in, it was lunchtime.
Their teachers made them sit and eat their sandwiches before they could see the animals.
"At this rate, we won't see anything," said Joe.
"I'm afraid we haven't very long," said the teacher.
"You must all be back at the coach in an hour."
Finn wanted to see the rhinos, and Joe wanted to see the lions.
Finally Joe won, and they rushed to the Big Cat Enclosure.
Joe had a horrible shock.
There was a barrier with a sign.
It said "Due to Cleaning, the Big Cat Enclosure is Closed Today."
"Oh well," said Finn. "We've got time to look at the rhinos if we run."
Joe was very quiet all the way back to school.
"How was the wildlife park?" asked Dad at tea.
"Did you see lots of animals?"
"Well..." said Joe. "I'm going this weekend," said Bella.
"You know what," Joe said, "I think I'll come too." "Hooray!" Bella yelled.

title: Joe & Bella: Rainy day
sourceTitle: Rainy day - The Storytellers
description: Mưa cả ngày, không đi biển được — Bella làm "bánh" cho chú chó Selby (thức ăn cho chó + cornflakes!). Từ vựng: pouring, sheeting down, queasy, make the best of it, sprinkles.

segments.text: One weekend, Mum had to work a shift at the hospital, and Dad had loads of marking to do,
which meant that neither of them had time to look after Joe and Bella.
But Joe and Bella didn't mind.
They were going to spend the weekend with Gran, and Gran had promised to take them to the beach!
There was just one problem.
When they woke up on Saturday morning, and looked out of the window, the rain was sheeting down!
Bella pressed her nose against the glass and said hopefully, "We can still go, can't we?"
But when Gran arrived to collect them, it was still pouring,
and Gran said they would just have to spend the day at her house instead.
It rained and rained. They watched a movie on TV, and when they stopped it was still raining.
They played cards with Gran, and when they stopped it was still raining.
They did some homework, ready for Monday, and when they stopped - it was still raining!
They tried taking Gran's dog, Selby, for a walk, but when they opened the door,
Selby took one look, whined, and ran back inside again!
Eventually, Gran went off to do some housework.
Joe decided to do more homework.
He had tests coming up at school and Mum and Dad were always on at him to work harder.
But Bella was too little to worry about tests.
"I'm bored," she said. "I hate this weather!"
"There's nothing we can do about it," said Joe.
"You'll just have to make the best of it."
Bella stomped off. Joe wasn't paying much attention to her, he was too busy with his maths.
After a while, though, he noticed a banging and thumping from the kitchen.
What was Bella up to?
He got up and looked round the door.
Bella was mixing something in a huge mixing bowl.
"What's that?" Joe asked. "It's a lovely cake," said Bella happily.
"But you can't have any."
"That's a relief," said Joe. "Because it looks terrible. And it smells worse!"
The cake mixture had all kinds of lumps in it and the smell was like no cake that Joe had ever smelled before!
"It's not for humans," said Bella. "It's for dogs."
"I've made it specially for Selby, because he couldn't go for his walk."
"What's it got in it?" Joe asked.
"Dog food," said Bella. "Silly!"
"And it's got cornflakes, because Selby loves cornflakes."
"And yogurt, because Selby loves yogurt."
"And toast and biscuits and tinned rice pudding."
Joe was feeling queasy just thinking about it.
"Well, I hope Selby likes it," he said.
But Selby didn't like it.
When Bella put it down on the floor for him to eat (raw, because she said it would taste better that way), Selby took one sniff and then ran out of the room!
Bella burst into tears. Gran came running into the kitchen.
"Oh dear, what is the matter, Bella?" she asked.
"It's raining," Bella howled. "It's never going to stop!"
"We can't go to the beach!"
"And now Selby doesn't like my cake!"
Joe didn't say anything, but he knew how Bella felt.
It was turning into a horrible day.
"Now then," said Gran. "Things aren't that bad."
"Why don't we do something to cheer ourselves up?" "Like what?" sniffed Bella.
"How about we make a cake as a surprise for your parents?"
"A cake for humans, not for dogs?"
"After all, they've been working hard all day."
"Can we eat some too?" asked Bella.
"Of course you can," said Gran.
"And can it be chocolate sponge?" asked Joe.
"With chocolate fudge icing?" asked Bella. "And sprinkles?"
"It certainly can," said Gran.
They had a lovely time making the cake.
And when they had finished decorating it, they suddenly realised that it wasn't raining any more.
They had been so busy they hadn't even noticed.
"Quick, let's get out while the sun's shining!" said Gran.
They took Selby down to the park, and when they got back, Mum and Dad had arrived.
Everybody was just ready for a slice of cake!

title: Joe & Bella: Car journey
sourceTitle: Car journey - The Storytellers
description: "Are we nearly there yet?" — chuyến đi xe lên Scotland: chơi I Spy, kẹt xe, lạc đường ở ngã tư và Bella chỉ đúng hướng. Từ vựng: traffic jam, service station, crossroads, signpost.

segments.text: "Are we nearly there yet?" asked Bella, banging her feet against the back of Mum's seat.
Joe, who was sitting next to her, groaned.
"That's the tenth time she's asked that."
"And there's still miles to go."
The Hobson family were off to Scotland to visit Nana and Gramps.
It was school holidays, and they were going to spend a whole week there.
They had crammed all their suitcases into the car and said goodbye to their friends and to Granny,
who was going to look after their pets while they were away.
Now, Bella and Joe were sitting in the back seat. But Bella was bored.
"Why don't you have a nap, Bella?" suggested Dad. "I'm not sleepy!"
"Why not watch another film on your tablet?" "Don't want to."
"Let's play I Spy," said Mum. "You start, Joe."
Bella always enjoyed playing this game.
Joe had to choose something that he could see, and everyone else had to guess what it was.
Joe looked around and saw some cows grazing in a field.
"I spy with my little eye, something beginning with C."
"Car," guessed Mum. "No." "Camper van," guessed Dad.
"No." "Cloud?" guessed Bella. "No." "What is it then?"
"Cow," said Joe. "But I can't see any cows," said Bella, looking around.
"Well, no," Joe admitted. "We've gone past now."
"But there was a field of cows before."
Bella wasn't pleased. So Joe let her have a turn.
The trouble was, they soon ran out of things to "I spy".
There wasn't much to see, apart from fields and hedges, the road in front of them, and the traffic going past.
So it was a great relief when Dad suddenly said, "I spy coffee,"
and Mum turned the car off the motorway and into a motorway service station.
Having a snack cheered everybody up.
Then they put more petrol in the car.
"It won't be long now," said Mum as they set off.
But as Dad drove towards the motorway, they got a terrible shock.
There were cars as far as the eye could see, and none of them was moving.
It was a giant traffic jam.
"There must be roadworks," said Mum.
"It's going to take hours," said Joe.
Dad turned the car around.
"We won't go on the motorway."
"We'll take the small roads instead."
"But we don't know the way," Mum said.
"We'll use our phones. They will show us the way!"
They drove into the hills.
There were no more cars.
There was no traffic at all.
The trouble was, soon there was no phone reception either!
"I knew this was a bad idea," said Mum.
"Nonsense," said Dad. "I know where we're going!"
Bella fell asleep. The roads grew narrower and turned into country lanes.
Eventually, they arrived at a crossroads.
"Now what?" said Mum. "Left or right or straight ahead?"
"Hmm," said Dad. "We're lost," said Mum.
"Admit it! There's nobody to ask, either."
Mum and Dad started squabbling.
Joe sat and wondered what they should do.
He had no idea which way led to Scotland.
The only good thing was that Bella was still asleep,
so at least he didn't have to listen to her complaining, and asking how long it would be.
Suddenly, Bella woke up. "Are we nearly there yet?"
"No," said Joe. "We don't know which way to go."
Bella pointed out the window.
"That way!" she said firmly.
Dad started the car and drove the way that Bella had pointed.
"But she's just guessing!" Joe said.
"She sounds very sure," said Dad.
"After all, we have to go somewhere!"
They hadn't travelled far when Mum gave a cry.
"Look! A signpost! Bella was right!" Joe had to laugh.
It might have been a lucky guess, but still, if it weren't for Bella, they would still be arguing at the crossroads.
"Are we nearly there yet?" Bella asked.
"Yes," said Joe, "this time we really are!"

title: Consonant + vowel: "an egg" → "anegg"
sourceTitle: Tim's pronunciation workshop: Consonant - vowel linking
description: Quy tắc nối âm cơ bản nhất: từ trước kết thúc bằng PHỤ ÂM, từ sau bắt đầu bằng NGUYÊN ÂM → đọc liền như một từ. "an egg" → /ənɛg/, "He's in the garden", "give up", "had it in".

segments.text: Today, I'm going to tell you about perhaps the most common feature of fluent English pronunciation.
And to help me, I'm going to use one of these.
Now, I know you know what it is, but let's ask the people of London to describe it.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
An egg - that's two words, right?
But, when we pronounce them, there's no gap in between them.
It almost sounds like one word.
Listen again. He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
He's holding an egg.
In fluent English, when one word ends in a consonant sound and the next word begins in a vowel sound,
we link the two sounds together without a pause in between them.
So, an egg becomes anegg.
This is called catenation.
Here are some more examples.
He's in the garden.
I used to believe in Father Christmas, but not any more.
I had to give up jogging.
He had it in his office.
Right, so you've heard the examples: you know the drill.
Listen and repeat.
He's in the garden.
I used to believe in Father Christmas, but not any more.
I had to give up jogging.
He had it in his office.

title: Linking /w/: "the shoe is" → "the shoe-w-is"
sourceTitle: Pronunciation: Linking /w/
description: Từ trước kết thúc bằng âm /uː/ (shoe, do, clue, glue), từ sau bắt đầu bằng nguyên âm → chen một âm /w/ nhẹ: "The shoe-w-is on the wrong foot", "do-w-I", "clue-w-at all".

segments.text: When we speak English fluently we sometimes add extra sounds in between the words to help them link together.
Now, have a look at my feet.
What's wrong with this?
Let's ask the people of London: The shoe is on the other foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
'Shoe' ends in the sound /u:/ and 'is' begins with the sound /ɪ/. But can you hear another sound linking them together?
Have another listen: The shoe is on the other foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
The shoe is on the wrong foot.
When one word ends in an /u:/ sound
and the next begins in a vowel sound we can just about hear another sound in between.
This sound is a bit like /w/.
So 'The shoe is' becomes 'The shoewis'.
This is called the linking /w/ - but it's important to remember that it's not a full /w/ sound.
It happens because the mouth moves from an /u:/ sound to a vowel sound
and on the way it passes through the /w/ mouth shape.
Here are some more examples: When do I have to be there?
I haven't got a clue at all.

title: Linking /j/: "I always" → "I-y-always"

description: Từ trước kết thúc bằng /aɪ/, /iː/, /eɪ/, /ɔɪ/ (I, the, lie, high), từ sau bắt đầu bằng nguyên âm → chen một âm /j/ nhẹ: "I-y-always", "the-y-end", "I-y-ate", "high-y-up".

title: Elision: the disappearing /d/ — "boiled potatoes"

description: Âm /d/ kẹp giữa hai phụ âm thường bị nuốt: "boiled potatoes" → "boil potatoes", "best friend", "hold back", "rolled down". Nghe khảo sát vui: khoai tây hấp hay luộc?

segments.text: Today, we're going to talk about one of the most important questions in contemporary Britain.

In the evening.

Now they all used the past form of the verb 'to be' - was.
Now the word 'was' is made of the sounds /w/, /ɒ/, /z/, isn't it?

I was laying in bed.
I was invited to a dinner at my friend's house.
I was playing football.
I was out drinking.
When the word 'was' is unstressed, as in the examples we've just heard,
then the vowel sound changes to a schwa, /ə/. So 'was' becomes /wəz/, and also 'were' becomes /wə/.
These are called weak forms.
Here are some more examples.
I was there when it happened.
We were delighted with the results.
We were having a good time until it rained.

title: "I'd have" → "I'd've": weak "have"
sourceTitle: Pronunciation: How to pronounce 'have' when it's an auxiliary
description: "have" làm trợ động từ đọc yếu thành /əv/: "I'd've missed the bus", "should've been", "would've done", "might've made" — rất hay gặp trong câu điều kiện loại 3.

segments.text: Phew, just made it.

Well, you know it's a really big garden.

So, let's ask some people in London what they would do if their alarms hadn't gone off this morning.
If my alarm hadn't gone off this morning, I'd've missed the bus.
I'd've stayed home.
I'd've woken up anyway.
I'd've been late for work.
I'd've missed the train.
I'd've stayed in bed.
In an earlier video we saw that the verb 'have' is pronounced /hæf/ when it's used in its modal form.
But this isn't the only way the pronunciation of 'have' can change.
Watch and listen again.
Can you hear how they pronounce it differently?
If my alarm hadn't gone off this morning, I'd've missed the bus.
I'd've stayed home.
I'd've woken up anyway.
I'd've been late for work.
I'd've missed the train.
I'd've stayed in bed.
When the verb have is used as an auxiliary it's often contracted.
And when it comes after a consonant sound it's pronounced /əv/.
So, 'I'd have been late' becomes 'I'd've been late'.
Now, this pronunciation is very common in conditional sentences, but it's not the only time you'll hear it.
Here are some more examples.
Your parcel should've been delivered yesterday.
I would've done it differently.
We might've made a mistake.
The police've arrived.
Right, so you've heard the examples, and now it's your turn.

I would've done it differently.
We might've made a mistake.
The police've arrived.

title: Weak form of "been": /biːn/ → /bɪn/
sourceTitle: Pronunciation: How fluent speakers pronounce 'been'
description: "been" không nhấn đọc ngắn là /bɪn/ (như "bin"): "I've /bɪn/ in London seven years", "How long have you /bɪn/ waiting?", "It's /bɪn/ years since…".

segments.text: Today, I'm going to use two things to help me demonstrate a feature of English pronunciation.
This is a bin and this is a bean.
What's the connection?
Well, I'm sure you know the past participle of the verb 'to be' - 'been', right?
Well, we asked some people how long they had been in London.
I've been in London seventeen years.
I have been in London seven years.
I've been in London for more than a year now.
I've been in London every summer since I was eighteen.
Now, they all used the word 'been' - but nobody actually said 'been'.
Listen again. What word do you actually hear them say?
I've been in London seventeen years.
I have been in London seven years.
I've been in London for more than a year now.
I've been in London every summer since I was eighteen.
In fluent everyday English, when the auxiliary 'been' is not stressed its pronunciation changes to /bɪn/.
'I've been in London since 2015' becomes 'I've /bɪn/ in London since 2015'.
This is what's known as a weak form and it helps speech to flow more naturally and fluently.
Here are some more examples.
I've been working here for several years.
How long have you been waiting?
It's been years since I went to the cinema.
What have you been up to since we last met?
So you've heard the examples, and now it's your turn.
You know the drill: listen and repeat.
I've been working here for several years.
How long have you been waiting?
It's been years since I went to the cinema.
What have you been up to since we last met?

title: Two ways to say "the": /ðə/ and /ðiː/
sourceTitle: Pronunciation: Two different ways to pronounce the English word 'the'
description: "the" + phụ âm đọc /ðə/ ("the blue one"), "the" + nguyên âm đọc /ðiː/ và nối /j/ ("the-y-orange one", "the apple pie", "the autumn").

you listen again and see if you can hear the two different ways the definite article is pronounced.

If it's not stressed, the pronunciation of the word 'the' will change depending on the word that follows.
If the next word begins in a consonant sound, it's pronounced /ðə/. I prefer the blue one.
But, if the next word begins in a vowel sound, it's pronounced /ðiː/. I prefer the orange one.
And you might remember from a previous video that when the sound /iː/ is followed by a vowel sound,
you might also hear a small linking /j/ in between.
I prefer the orange one.
Here are some more examples.

I think the autumn is the best time of year.
The earlier I get up, the happier I am.
It's the one over there.
So you've heard the examples, and now it's your turn.

title: Linking drill: 5 sentences, find the links
